Numbers: Chapter one. How a number is made.

A statistic is not observed; it is made, and remade. America's first estimate of a quarter's GDP comes about a month after the quarter ends, built partly from complete data and partly from assumptions where the data are not in yet. A second and a third estimate follow, then annual revisions as tax and census data arrive, then comprehensive revisions that can rewrite decades. Payrolls come from a survey of more than a hundred thousand employers, a week after the month ends, with a model of businesses born and dying that the survey cannot yet see. Each month's number is revised twice, and once a year the whole series is benchmarked to the unemployment-insurance tax records. Those benchmarks can be large. In August 2024 the Bureau of Labor Statistics announced that the year to March had about 818 thousand fewer jobs than reported, later settled at 598 thousand; in 2025 the first announcement was 911 thousand; in 2026, 79 thousand.

How much do the numbers move? Here is every quarter since the mid-1960s: its annualized growth as first published, against what today's data say. If nothing were ever revised, every dot would sit on the dashed line. They cluster around it, with a correlation of 0.89, but the average revision is 1.48 points either way, and on average growth has been revised up by 0.44. In 17 quarters, in red, the first estimate had the wrong sign: growth became a fall, or a fall growth. Gregory Mankiw and Matthew Shapiro asked in 1986 whether such revisions are news or noise; for American GDP they found mostly news, which means the first number is the best guess at the time, but a guess.

The quarter that mattered most shows why. The first estimate of the last quarter of 2008, published in January 2009 while Congress debated a stimulus, was minus 3.8 percent a year: bad, but not catastrophic. Vintage by vintage it got worse. Today it is minus 8.5: more than twice as bad. Policy was made with the first number.
Seasonal: Every January, America loses millions of jobs. These are monthly changes in payrolls before adjustment, 2015 to 2019: every January a fall of two to three million, as Christmas jobs end, then a rise through the spring, a dip in July, a rise in the autumn. The swings have a standard deviation of 0.9 million a month. The adjusted series, in orange, which the news reports, removes the pattern that repeats every year and moves by about 208 thousand. Nearly everything a viewer hears about jobs has been through this filter.

How is it done? Julius Shiskin's X-11 method, developed at the Census Bureau in the 1960s, still sits inside the programmes statistical agencies use. Take logs. Estimate the trend with a centred twelve-month average, which cancels any pattern that repeats every year. What is left is the season plus noise. Average each calendar month's value over neighbouring years, so Januaries are compared with Januaries. Subtract that seasonal factor. Run on unadjusted payrolls, this simplified version finds January's factor 1.5 percent below the year's average, and December's 1.0 percent above; its monthly changes differ from the official ones by 85 thousand, on average, before 2020.

What can it invent? In April 2020 payrolls fell by 20.5 million. The filter as described averages each April with its neighbours, so that one collapse leaks into the seasonal factor for April in every year around it: by 2020 it is minus 3.4 percent, an April slump that never recurs. X-11 guards against this by leaving extreme values out of the seasonal averages; done here, April's factor barely moves. The difference is not small: in April 2021 the two adjustments differ by 3.3 million jobs. After 2020 the version without the outlier step misses the official monthly changes by 682 thousand on average; with it, by 73. The statistical agencies spent 2020 and 2021 deciding, month by month, which movements were seasons and which were history.
PlayIt: Chapter three. Play it: nowcast the quarter.

Your turn. This is the Island, in the first days of a quarter. Four monthly indicators arrive at different times: payrolls, industrial production, retail sales and a business survey, which comes out first. Before the quarter starts, the six months behind us look ordinary, apart from one weak month for retail, and the nowcast for the quarter's growth is 1.1 percent a year, with a wide band. Then the survey for the first month arrives, and it is weak: the nowcast drops to minus 0.3. Will GDP fall this quarter? Decide now, with what you have.

Here is what came next. The first month's payrolls, production and retail sales confirm the survey: the nowcast falls to minus 2.9, and the chance of a fall passes 91 percent. The second month leaves little doubt, and the third settles it. When the quarter's GDP is finally published, it fell at minus 3.9 percent a year. If you said 'fall' after the survey, you were early and right; most forecasters wait for the hard data, and many wait for the GDP release itself. A nowcast is this: a forecast of the present, updated every time a number comes out.
Nowcast: The oldest nowcasting tool is the bridge equation. Regress GDP growth on the quarterly averages of a few monthly indicators, here payrolls and industrial production, which come out within weeks. In the middle of a quarter some months are missing; fill them with each indicator's own forecast. Nowcasters call this the ragged edge. Run it on American data since 1985, refitting each quarter on the past only. Before the quarter, a simple autoregression in GDP misses by 2.24 points on average; after one month of indicators, by 2.01; after two, 1.88; after all three, 1.71. These use today's revised data with the release calendar imposed, pseudo real time, so a nowcaster at the time would have done somewhat worse.

The method central banks use now is a dynamic factor model, after James Stock and Mark Watson, run through the Kalman filter, as Domenico Giannone, Lucrezia Reichlin and David Small showed in 2008. One unseen factor, the state of the economy, moves slowly from month to month. Each monthly indicator is that factor plus its own noise. And GDP growth is the quarter's average of the factor, plus noise. The Kalman filter, Part fifty-five's tool, simply skips whatever has not been released, so the ragged edge costs nothing. On the Island, where the model is true, the error falls from 3.04 before the quarter to 1.06 once all three months are in, and the bands are honest: one standard deviation covers about two thirds of outcomes. Every revision of the nowcast can be split into the news in each release, what came out minus what was expected, times a weight. That is how a nowcaster explains a revision: the news in the payroll number moved us by this much. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow, since 2014, and the New York Fed's staff nowcast, first published in 2016, publish exactly such numbers.
Signals: Chapter five. The yield curve and the Sahm rule.

The most famous recession signal is the slope of the yield curve. In pink, the ten-year Treasury yield minus the three-month bill rate, with the recessions shaded. Before almost every recession since the 1960s, it went below zero: long rates under short ones, an inverted curve. Arturo Estrella and Frederic Mishkin turned it into a probability with a probit: the chance that the economy is in recession twelve months from now, given today's slope. Fitted to every month since 1959, it ranks recession months above others 82 percent of the time. Count the inversions that lasted at least three months: 9. 7 were followed by a recession within two years; the exceptions are 1966 and the long inversion of 2022 to 2024. And one of the hits, 2019, was followed by a pandemic, which no yield curve predicted.

The second signal reads unemployment. Claudia Sahm proposed it in 2019 as a trigger for automatic payments to households: when the three-month average unemployment rate rises half a point above its lowest in the previous year, a recession has almost always begun. Computed with the unemployment rates known at the time, the rule has fired 11 times since 1960. Most signals came within a few months of a recession's start. Two did not: in 1976, and in 2024. It is a rule for recognizing a recession early, not for forecasting one, and like every rule fitted to a few events, it can break.

And then came the alarms of 2022 to 2024. The yield curve inverted for 25 months, the longest inversion in the data. The probit's chance of recession peaked at 58 percent. In the spring of 2023 the median professional forecaster put a 50 percent chance on a fall in output the next quarter. In July 2024 the Sahm rule fired. No recession has been dated since the pandemic's. The economy grew instead. The curve inverted because the Federal Reserve raised short rates fast to fight inflation, and the Sahm rule fired partly because unemployment rose as more people looked for work, not only because people lost jobs. Every signal is a summary of past recessions, and the next one need not look like them.
Scoring: How should a forecast be scored? The error is the forecast minus what happened. Its average is the bias; the square root of its average square, the root mean squared error, is the usual score. To ask whether one forecaster really beats another, Francis Diebold and Roberto Mariano took the difference in their squared errors and asked whether its mean is zero, with a standard error that allows for the errors' correlation over time. Three rules make the scoring fair. Score against what could be known: the first estimate of the outcome, not today's revised one, which no forecaster could have aimed at. Forecasts a year ahead made each quarter overlap, so their errors are correlated. And always compare with a benchmark that takes no skill.

Here are America's professional forecasters, scored that way: every median forecast of real GDP growth since 1968, for the current quarter and up to four quarters ahead, against the first published number. The two quarters of the pandemic, with swings of thirty points, are left out. For the current quarter their error is 1.86 points, rising to 2.78 two quarters ahead and 2.97 a year ahead. The benchmark that takes no skill, the average growth of the last ten years, misses by about 3.1 at every horizon. Repeating last quarter's number does worse still. So the forecasters beat the average, by Diebold and Mariano's test, for the current quarter and the next 2 quarters. Beyond that, their forecasts are no better than the average of the past. And they lean optimistic: a year ahead the average error is 0.72 points. The honest summary is that economists can read the present, and a little of the next six months; beyond that, the forecast is mostly the average.
Record: Who forecasts best? In 2000 Christina and David Romer compared the Federal Reserve staff's forecasts, in the Greenbook prepared for each policy meeting and published five years later, with commercial forecasters', and found the staff's inflation forecasts better. Here is that comparison redone for 1968 to 2020: forecasts of GDP-price inflation made in the same quarter. The staff's errors are smaller at every horizon, significantly so from 3 quarters ahead. The Romers' reading was that the Federal Reserve knows things the market does not, which is why markets watch what it does so closely.

Did anyone see the recessions coming? Each quarter the professional forecasters give the chance that output falls the next quarter. Here it is in the quarter before each American recession since 1970, and at its highest once the recession had begun. Before, mostly between ten and forty percent; only once, in 1980, above a half. Once inside, they recognized it. The famous misses are the same story: in August 2008 the median forecaster expected growth of 1.5 percent in 2009, which shrank by 2.6; in June 2021 the Federal Reserve projected inflation of 2.1 percent for 2022, which came in at 6.1. Across 63 countries, as the opening showed, it is the same: recessions are recognized, not forecast.
Hard: Chapter eight. Why recessions are hard to forecast.

Why is it so hard? Start with James Hamilton's model of 1989. The economy is in one of two states: expansion, with growth around 3 percent a year, or recession, around minus 3. Expansions persist with probability 0.95 a quarter, recessions with 0.75. Here is a simulated history, recessions shaded. Hamilton's filter infers the state from growth alone. It finds 169 of the 177 recessions, but on average 0.4 quarters after they began: recognizing, again, rather than forecasting.

Now suppose a forecaster knew the model exactly, and even knew today's state for certain. From inside an expansion, the best forecast is positive at every horizon. From inside a recession, it is negative for a couple of quarters, then positive, because recessions end. So the forecast that minimizes squared error is below zero a year ahead in none of the quarters, though growth is negative in 22 percent of them. The real forecasters do the same: their forecasts a year ahead were below zero 0 percent of the time, and growth was negative in 13 percent of quarters. This is not cowardice. When an event is rare and its timing random, the best guess of the average is never the event.

And there is a second difficulty, which weather forecasters do not have. A forecast of recession, if believed, can lead a central bank to cut rates and firms to hold back, which can make the recession milder, or prevent it, and then the forecast looks wrong. Robert Lucas's critique, from Part twenty-eight, applies to forecasts too: when people act on a prediction, the pattern it was fitted to can change. Some of 2023's missing recession may be of this kind; no one can say how much.
Text: Words can be counted. Scott Baker, Nicholas Bloom and Steven Davis count, each month, the share of articles in ten leading American newspapers that use a word about the economy, a word about policy, and a word about uncertainty, all together, and scale it so that the 1985 to 2009 average is one hundred. The index jumps at the moments you would expect: the debt-ceiling standoff of 2011, the government shutdown of 2019, the pandemic and the election of 2020. Its highest month in four decades is 2025's April, at 460, when sweeping tariffs were announced. The index does more than describe: investment and hiring fall when it rises, in firms more exposed to government spending most of all.

Text reaches further. Stephen Hansen, Michael McMahon and Andrea Prat read the transcripts of the Federal Reserve's policy meetings with topic models. After 1993, when members learned that the transcripts would be published, newer members came better prepared, citing more data, and also conformed more, disagreeing less: transparency changed the deliberation it revealed. The methods have moved from counting words to dictionaries, topic models, and now the embeddings of language models, which place documents in a space of meanings; Matthew Gentzkow, Bryan Kelly and Matt Taddy survey them. The old rules still apply: a measure built from text is a measure, to be checked against the careful numbers, and as easy to overfit as any other.
Judgment: Chapter eleven. Judgment, models and combinations.

If two forecasts are both informative, why choose? In 1969 John Bates and Clive Granger showed that a weighted average of two forecasts can beat both, when their errors are not perfectly correlated. Take the staff's and the professional forecasters' inflation forecasts from the last chapter. For the current quarter, half and half has the lowest error, 0.94, and the best weight on the staff is about 0.55. Further ahead the two forecasts' errors are correlated 0.94, the staff's are smaller, and the best weight goes to 1.00: averaging only helps when the forecasters know different things. In practice, James Stock and Mark Watson found that simple averages usually beat weights estimated from a short history, the forecast-combination puzzle: estimated weights fit the past too well.

Models are never left alone. Forecasters adjust them by judgment, for a strike, a storm, a pandemic, or news the model has never seen; the adjustment should be written down, and scored like any forecast. And one number is often less useful than a few coherent stories: what happens if oil doubles, or credit tightens, and what policy each would call for. In April 2024 Ben Bernanke, asked to review the Bank of England's forecasting after it missed the inflation of 2021 and 2022, made twelve recommendations: rebuild the models and data, publish alternative scenarios, and drop the fan chart the Bank had used for nearly thirty years. Which brings us to how uncertainty should be told.
Uncertainty: Chapter twelve. Telling people about uncertainty.

A forecast without its uncertainty invites false confidence. Here is the latest professional forecast, from the survey of the fourth quarter of 2026: growth of about 2.3 percent a year, and about 2.1 a year on. Around it, the forecasters' own record: the band holding half of their past errors at each horizon, and the band holding nine in ten. A year ahead the wider band runs from minus 4.2 to 5.5 percent. Read that way, the record says there is about a 21 percent chance that growth a year ahead will be negative, though the forecast itself will never say so. The Bank of England has drawn its forecasts this way since 1996, as a fan.

How to say it in words? The climate scientists of the IPCC tie their words to numbers: 'likely' means a probability of at least two in three. Fan charts have a known weakness: readers look at the centre and ignore the edges; Bernanke judged that they conveyed little useful information, and recommended scenarios instead. Scenarios have the opposite weakness: they tell stories without saying which is likeliest. The practical rule is simple: give the number, the range, and what would change your mind.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: forecast errors by horizon.

This part opens a new Dial: how far ahead the economy can be read. The professional forecasters miss the current quarter's growth by 1.86 points, the next by 2.47, and a year ahead by 2.97. The benchmark that takes no skill, the last ten years' average, misses by 3.06. The status is settled within a range: the present can be read, the next six months a little, and beyond that the forecast is mostly the average. For policy, that means what matters most is not the forecast but how quickly it is revised, which is the whole case for nowcasting.
